Public GPU prices held; regional catalog visibility shifted. The transaction benchmark was again moving this week.

Ornn's H100 SXM index saw the largest seven-day percentage move among the four tracked GPU families, settling on September 14 at $2.75 per GPU-hour, approximately 13.2% below its September 7 reading. # Cloud GPU Price Index

A daily record of what secure on-demand cloud GPUs cost per GPU-hour, computed from the current offers GPUPerHour tracks across cloud GPU providers. Published as a table and as CSV; no charts yet.

## What this index measures

Every day at 00:05 UTC the index records, for each of the 13 GPUs in the basket, the minimum, median and maximum price per GPU-hour across every current offer on the site. An offer is current only when all of the following hold:

- the provider reports it as available right now;
- the provider has live stock tracking, so "available" is a real-time observation, not a catalog entry;
- it was seen within the last 15 minutes;
- it is secure on-demand pricing on provider-operated data-center hardware, billed per GPU-hour;
- spot, interruptible, reserved and peer-to-peer or marketplace listings are excluded.

13 GPUs chosen to cover training, inference, workstation and consumer segments across more than one provider. Membership only changes with a new basket version, so series are never compared across versions silently.

results.title: The 70% H100 Price Crash: Neo-Clouds vs AWS Egress Tax
highlights:
I track GPU rental pricing for a living. Every week I pull rate cards from six cloud providers, run them through a TCO model, and send a digest to engineering leads deciding where to put their next training run. And I want to be direct with you about what I’m seeing in September 2026: the H100 market has bifurcated. Neo-clouds collapsed from $8.50 per GPU-hour in 2023 down to $3.99 per GPU-hour on RunPod today — a 53% drop in three years. AWS’s `p5.48xlarge` list price sits at $55.04 per node-hour ($6.88 per GPU-hour) — and once you model egress taxes, FSx Lustre storage, NAT Gateway transit, and mandatory support tiers, the real all-in rate climbs past $9.85 per GPU-hour. That spread is not a pricing anomaly. It is a deliberate infrastructure tax, and most engineering teams are still paying it without questioning it.

...

Quick-Answer: H100 True Cost, September 2026

 Neo-cloud H100 on-demand pricing reached $3.99 per GPU-hour (RunPod Secure Cloud) in September 2026 — down 53% from the 2023 peak of $8.50–$10.00 per GPU-hour. CoreWeave on-demand is $6.16 per GPU-hour ($49.24/8-GPU node); with a 1-year reserved contract (up to 60% discount), effective rates reach approximately $2.46 per GPU-hour. AWS p5.48xlarge lists at $6.88 per GPU-hour ($55.04 per node) — but with egress ($0.09 per GB), FSx Lustre storage, NAT Gateway overhead, and enterprise support surcharges, all-in effective rates exceed $9.85 per GPU-hour. Key architectural trade-off: CoreWeave’s NVIDIA Quantum-2 InfiniBand delivers 50%+ MFU on large clusters vs. RunPod RoCEv2’s ~34% MFU, making provider choice a topology decision, not just a billing comparison.

...

Catalyst 1: The Blackwell Migration. NVIDIA’s B200 and GB200 NVL72 rack-scale systems began volume delivery in late 2025. OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and xAI — the tier-1 buyers who were paying $8+ per hour for H100 access — migrated their frontier training runs to Blackwell. That mass departure offloaded vast H100 & H200 cluster inventories into secondary rental pools overnight.

results.title: The Practitioner's Guide to the Compute Future (Part 1)
highlights:
Updated September 8, 2026. Index and curve values as of September 7, 2026.

If you run 50 H100s around the clock, you pay a little under $100,000 a month at today's rate, and you have no idea what you will pay next June. From October 5, pending regulatory review, you can find out. That is the practical meaning of the two compute futures contracts NYMEX is listing on Silicon Data's H100 and B200 rental indices, and this piece is about how a company that has never traded a future would actually use one.

## The contract, in five facts

The CME notice sets out two contracts: Silicon Data H100 Rental Index Futures, code GPU1, and Silicon Data B200 Rental Index Futures, code GPU2. Five things matter for a user.

One contract is 730 GPU-hours. That number is 365 days times 24 hours divided by 12, the hours in an average month, so one contract is one GPU for one month. Sizing a hedge is counting GPUs.

Prices are quoted in dollars and cents per GPU-hour, the same unit as your invoice and the same unit as the index. The smallest move is one cent; one tick translates to $7.30 of P&L per contract.

Settlement is financial. No GPU changes hands; money does.

Trading in a contract ends on the last business day of its month, and 36 monthly contracts are listed at a time, so you can cover any month up to three years out: stack the monthly contracts for the months you need, and the stack is your hedge.

The exchange fee is $5.50 per contract for non-members. Your broker adds its own.

...

As currently announced, GPU1 for a given month settles against the Silicon Data H100 Rental Index averaged over that month, not the index on one day.

The reason for averaging is that compute behaves like electricity, not like oil. A GPU-hour is consumed the hour it exists; it cannot be stored and delivered later. Your bill is not one price on one day, it is the sum of every day's rate across the month. A contract that settles on the month's average tracks that bill.

highlights:
## Abstract

Canonical source: https://gpueconomy.com/price-index, recomputed hourly. This record is a dated snapshot (version 2026-09-14, data updated 2026-09-14T08:38:28.803126+00:00) so that a cited number keeps existing exactly as it was cited. Please cite GPU Economy and link the page. The index is the weekly median publicly listed on-demand price of one NVIDIA H100 SXM GPU-hour across the cloud GPU providers tracked by GPU Economy, in US dollars per GPU per hour, with a chain-linked base-100 companion series that moves only when a provider changes a listed price. Two files, two panels, never merged: price-index.csv is GPU Economy's own series, read hourly from each provider's price page from the week of 2026-09-07 (2 weeks in this version); price-index-history.csv is a second-hand series reconstructed from the public skypilot-org/skypilot-catalog (Apache 2.0) for the weeks before that (88 weeks, at most 7 providers). price-index.json carries the current week's constituents with the source URL behind every quote. Method: median, not mean, over one quote per provider and region (a provider that lists several regions enters once per region, and weighting_check in the JSON recomputes each week as a median of per-provider medians); on-demand rates only, spot and reserved excluded; node-priced offers divided by GPU count; USD-listed quotes only; marketplace floors excluded; a week is published only when at least 8 providers contributed. Full method: https://gpueconomy.com/methodology. Field definitions are in the README included with the files.

results.title: GPU as a Service Is Being Rebuilt From the Ground Up. Here's What the Infrastructure Shift Actually Means. - Kayla Technology Advisors
highlights:
### 2. Neoclouds Are Winning on Cost, Then Moving Up the Stack

The neocloud model, exemplified by CoreWeave, Nebius, Crusoe, and Vultr, exploits a structural cost advantage over hyperscalers: by eliminating general-purpose cloud software overhead and providing bare-metal GPU clusters, they can price 40% below hyperscaler rates on equivalent hardware.

Specialized inference providers like Together AI take the cost advantage further. By optimizing specifically for token delivery rather than general compute, they can price inference at roughly 80% below hyperscaler rates for equivalent output.

But raw compute margins are thin. A pure GPU leasing model delivers 20% to 30% gross margins, which is not a sustainable competitive position. The neoclouds that are building durable businesses are moving up the software stack, building custom hypervisors, AI orchestration platforms, and managed inference services that capture software-level margins. CoreWeave reported 113% cloud revenue growth in August 2026. Nebius grew cloud revenue more than five-fold. These growth rates reflect the demand for the cost-advantaged position, but the margin structure they are building toward is software, not hardware.
